chen: Quick follow-up to the paged-KV + attention kernel RFC. Ran a small prototype and hit a few compatibility gaps: kernel/eviction handshake, atomicity on page swaps, and fragmentation causing attention stalls. Wanted to surface concrete tradeoffs and a short rollout plan.

sarah: Can you enumerate failure modes you observed? I saw a tail spike in nightly tests but didn't dig in.

chen: Sure — two main failure modes we saw in the prototype:
1) mid-attention page miss: kernel expects a contiguous KV range, finds a hole (evicted block) and falls back to full recompute -> 30-70ms latency spike. Log snippet: `panic: missing_kv_block at layer 9 offset 8192`
2) fragmentation churn: many small blocks being evicted and reloaded causing cache thrash and increased GC/compaction work.

anya: For (1) what about a lightweight reservation/refcount system? On request start runtime increments refcount for needed blocks, prevents eviction while in-flight, decrement at completion. Cheap and avoids hard locks.

matt: Refcounts help but are tricky with async batching and multi-kernel pipelines. Suggest a reservation token model instead: `reserve_pages([p1,p2]) -> token` kernel uses token during compute; runtime refuses eviction if token present. Token can have TTL so misbehaving kernels don't pin forever.

chen: I like the token idea. Also think we should make kernel capability negotiation explicit so we don't have surprises at runtime. Example proto idea: 
```
caps = kernel.query_caps(model_name)
// caps: {"supports_blocked_kv": bool, "atomic_page_swap": bool, "max_contig_blocks": int}
if caps.supports_blocked_kv:
    runtime.bind_kernel(kernel, eviction_mode="block", reservation_api=true)
else:
    runtime.fallback_to_full_kv(kernel)
```
This makes kernel selection deterministic and keeps a safe fallback.

sarah: Eviction policy also needs work. Block-level LRU + hysteresis to avoid oscillation seems reasonable. If fragmentation ratio > 0.3, trigger compaction/backfill. But compaction must be low-priority and incremental.

anya: Compaction = heavy. Can we do opportunistic defragmentation: when loading a block, try to coalesce adjacent hot blocks into a contiguous region if free memory available. Also prefer migrating hot prefixes to a small hot-cache on-device to reduce misses.

matt: Operational plan thoughts:
1) Add kernel capability flags + reservation API (no functional change)
2) Runtime fallback to emulated full-KV path for kernels that don't support blocked KV
3) Add metrics: page_miss_count, reservation_contention, fragmentation_ratio, compaction_runs
4) Canary blocked-KV kernel on low-traffic canary, measure tail latency + miss amplification
5) Gradual rollout with auto-fallback if tail breaches SLO
This minimizes blast radius.

infra-bot: Deploy pipeline triggered: canary runtime + kernel flags branch -> https://ci.redwood/infer/1234 :rocket: (watch logs in infra/canary)

chen: Action items for next week:
- chen: prototype reservation token + kernel caps (will push draft PR)
- matt: add the page-level telemetry and canary dashboards
- sarah: author perf test harness that simulates long-prefix workloads and small-block churn
- anya: sketch opportunistic coalescing algorithm (pseudocode)

matt: One more tradeoff note — atomic_page_swap support in kernel avoids needing copy-on-write at runtime but increases kernel complexity and verification surface. If kernels can't implement atomic swap right away, use reservation + double-buffering in runtime as interim.

anya: Agreed. Double-buffering seems safe: load new blocks into a staging area then atomically flip pointer. Costs some memory but keeps kernel simple.

chen: Great. I'll open the PR with the reservation API + caps doc today and tag you all. Thanks for quick feedback. :+1:
